As shown in Figure III-10, Hardin will experience very substantial increases in enrollment over the 25 year period, ranging from 53 percent in the high school to 71 percent in the elementary school. The immediate upward changes expected in Hardin are much more rapid than will be experienced in the other schools, with one-third to one-half of the increase occuring by 1978. If coal development in addition to Westmore-land is seriously delayed, the increases in enrollment by that year will be somewhat smaller, and any major increases would occur at a later date. However, with or without other development, the impact of Westmoreland's most probable level of development (Scenario 1) would be considerable, particularly in 1979 when enrollments are projected to rise sharply, and in 1989 when enrollment would experience a temporary decline associated with decrease in construction employment. In other years, the enrollment increases are nearly steady.
Law and Order - Although no increase in crime rates has been observed in the area impacted by existing Westmoreland development, rapid urbanization has often been associated with alarming changes in crime rates. A Wyoming study found that during 1971-1973, counties impacted by coal development had increases in crime rates which were many times higher than the rest of the state. Wyoming considers this trend sufficiently critical to recommend that crime prevention in these counties be given special study and attention.
